title: The king's offer
hook: in Rajagaha King Bimbisara offers him wealth; he declines (Sn 3.1), and later tradition adds his promise to return if he finds the way

segments.voice: Yesterday, Kanthaka's heart: the white horse who, in the later telling, died of grief. Your line was they grieve too. Which animal did you treat gently? Day forty-one.

Rajagaha, capital of the kingdom of Magadha. A stranger with a shaved head walks from house to house with a bowl, eyes lowered, taking whatever is put in it. From his palace, King Bimbisara sees him, and something in the way this man walks makes the king send messengers after him. Turning down something bad is easy. Turning down something good, more money, a promotion, a place in someone's big plans, is a different kind of hard. That's what's coming on a hillside outside the city. Today, the king's offer.
screen: `A STRANGER WITH A BOWL.` → `THE KING WATCHES FROM ABOVE.` → `SAYING NO TO SOMETHING GOOD.`

segments.voice: This scene is in the Pali canon itself, in a poem in the Sutta Nipata called the Going Forth. The king notices that this beggar is no ordinary beggar. He walks mindfully, the poem says, eyes down, looking only a yoke's length ahead. His messengers find him on a hill outside the city, eating his alms food, and the king comes out in his chariot to meet him. And the king makes an offer. You're young, you're clearly of noble birth. Come and lead my army. Take wealth. Enjoy it. The wanderer answers calmly. He tells the king where he comes from: a people of the Himalayan foothills, the Sakyans. He says he didn't leave home looking for pleasures. He's seen the danger in them, and he sees safety in letting them go. I'm going to strive, he says. That's where my heart is. The poem ends there. The later commentaries add one more exchange, and it's the one people remember. The king says: then when you find what you're looking for, come back here first and teach me. And the wanderer promises he will. Tradition says he kept that promise, and the story will get there. What the scene shows is a no that isn't rude, bitter or proud. He declines a kingdom, kindly, and leaves the door open. A promise to come back is a way of saying: this no isn't about you. It's about the road.
screen: `A POEM IN THE SUTTA NIPATA.` · `A YOKE'S LENGTH AHEAD.` · `WEALTH, AN ARMY — AND A NO.` · `COME BACK AND TEACH ME.` · then, large: `A PROMISE TO COME BACK.`

segments.voice: Sit comfortably, and let the breath settle. Think of something you've been offered lately that you don't really want. An invitation, a task, one more commitment, a second helping. Picture yourself declining it the way the wanderer did: calm, warm, without a long excuse. Feel what it's like in the body to say no kindly. Not a wall. An open hand. If it helps, silently try the words: thank you, not this time. Then rest with the breath. The bell holds the time.
The king's offer. King Bimbisara offers the wanderer wealth and an army; he declines, and in the later telling, promises to come back.
Your line: a promise to come back. Today, decline one thing kindly, and if you can, leave the door open for another time. Day forty-one.

howItsDone: Buddhists remember King Bimbisara as one of the Buddha's great lay supporters, and the Pabbajja Sutta, the poem of this meeting, is still recited and studied as an early account of the going forth.

fork.setup: a king offers you wealth and command of his army. you're young, broke and sleeping on a hillside. what do you say?
options: no, kindly: I'm going to strive.
not now, but maybe in a year.
fork.reveal: he declines. he left home not for pleasure but to strive. in the commentaries, the king asks him to come back first when he finds the way, and he promises.

original.note: Pali: the name of the king of Magadha, who ruled from Rajagaha.

trapdoor: what you thought: a king tried to bribe a monk.
what it means: the wanderer turns down a kingdom kindly, without pride, and leaves the door open.
what a scholar hears: Sn 3.1 (Pabbajja Sutta) gives the meeting and refusal; the promise to return comes from the commentary, and the Vinaya later tells of Bimbisara becoming a follower.

sources.ref: Pabbajja Sutta (Sutta Nipata 3.1): Bimbisara's offer and the refusal

notes: Sn 3.1 paraphrased throughout (Fausbøll 1881 exists but its exact words are not quoted). Confirm the details: eyes down, a plow's (yoke's) length ahead, the Pandava hill, army and wealth offered, Sakyan answer.
The promise to return is attributed to the commentaries; confirm the source.
'Tradition says he kept that promise' previews the Bamboo Grove story without teaching it. Confirm.
Review pass: the hook credited the promise to return to Sn 3.1; reworded so the promise is credited to later tradition, matching the teach and the myth game.
